title: Generic interchange under M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D: the 'no substitution' instruction, the order of interchange and the hospital exemption
rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D requires every prescription issued in the commonwealth by a practitioner to meet the standards for format established by the Department of Public Health, and provides that only by signing the prescription in accordance with those standards does the practitioner validate it. The standards shall permit the practitioner to instruct the pharmacist to dispense a brand name drug product by indicating 'no substitution'; they shall require that the indication of 'no substitution' not be the default indication and that the prescription indicate 'Interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates "no substitution" in accordance with the law'. Where the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', the pharmacist shall dispense the exact drug product as indicated, or as written, by the practitioner. Except in cases where the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', the pharmacist shall dispense an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists or, if none exists, a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary or supplement thereof, and shall also indicate the fact of the interchange on the label in the form 'Interchange (name of exact drug product dispensed)'. The section defines an interchangeable drug product as a product containing a drug in the same amounts of the same active ingredients in the same dosage form as other products with the same generic or chemical name, and an interchangeable abuse deterrent drug product as a drug with abuse deterrent properties identified by the drug formulary commission as an appropriate substitute for a drug that the commission has determined poses a heightened level of risk to the public due to the drug's potential for abuse and misuse pursuant to M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(b). In the event of noncompliance by a pharmacist or a practitioner, the drug purchaser or patient may inform the director of consumer affairs and business regulation, who shall refer the matter to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and, where appropriate, to the Board of Registration in Medicine, for appropriate action. The provisions of the section do not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, provided that all outpatient prescriptions dispensed in a hospital shall be on prescription forms as required by the section and that no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.
exam_relevance: Tests the order the statute sets where 'no substitution' has not been indicated (an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists, otherwise a less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product allowed by the current formulary), that a 'no substitution' indication requires the exact product and so displaces both, and the hospital exemption together with its outpatient-form and retail-pharmacy provisos.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws, prescriptions of interchangeable drug products
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D, definitions through the hospital exemption paragraph

exceptions: Where the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', the pharmacist shall dispense the exact drug product as indicated by the practitioner; the interchange direction applies only in cases where 'no substitution' has not been indicated.

The provisions of M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D do not apply to prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51; all outpatient prescriptions dispensed in a hospital shall nevertheless be on prescription forms as required by the section, and no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.
common_confusions: Treating price as the first question. Where an interchangeable abuse deterrent product exists the statute directs that product, and its text attaches no price or availability qualifier to it; the less expensive, reasonably available interchangeable product is the direction where none exists.

Treating 'no substitution' as the default. The standards must make it a non-default indication, and the prescription itself states that interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates 'no substitution'.

Assuming that a pharmacy located in a hospital is exempt. The exemption reaches prescriptions dispensed in a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, and no retail pharmacy, however organized, is exempted.
verification_notes: Read in the current text of M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D on malegislature.gov on 2026-09-16, including the definitions stated in the section.
